paragraphs.text: ORDER AND RITE FOR THOSE WHO CONFESS, by our holy father John the Faster. [?] The priest takes the person who is about to confess and stands him in front of the altar. With him he chants the Trisagion and Psalm 6, "Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger"; Psalm 24, "To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul"; and Psalm 50, "Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy." Then he says the Glory. Then he says Psalm 31, "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven"; Psalm 69, "O God, attend to my help"; and Psalm 101 [?], "Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry [come to you]." Glory. Then he says the troparion in the fourth tone, "Visit my lowly soul." Another: "Sailing across the sea." "Let us run earnestly to the Mother of God." After this he also says the prayer given below. O Lord our God, Father and Master of all, who look upon all things, and who in your love for humankind grant forgiveness to those who turn to you from their own sins through repentance; who had mercy on David through his confession when he had sinned; who added years of life to Hezekiah when he wept and entreated your compassion; who accepted the repentance of Manasseh and freed him from such great evils; who granted pardon through tears to Peter and to the harlot; who justified the tax collector when he groaned; who opened a father's arms to the prodigal; who want all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, who rejoice over a sinner who repents, and who do not desire the death of the sinner but rather that he should turn and live: do you yourself, most good Savior, hear my prayer too, the prayer of your unworthy and useless servant. I am not worthy to call upon your all-holy name because of the multitude of my iniquities; but since I am invested with the dignity of the priesthood and, in keeping with your loving command, receive those who confess their offenses to you, I entreat you with fear and trembling. Hear me, then, a sinner, according to the multitude of your mercy, and accept your servant N., who is making his confession. And if he has committed any sin, voluntary or involuntary, in word or deed or thought, overlook it, for you are good. For you alone have authority to forgive sins, and before you we fall down, and you we entreat, and we sing your praises, glorifying you with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now, etc. After this he has the penitent make three genuflections with his head uncovered, doing the same himself; and when the penitent has risen, he instructs him as follows.

It is not I, my spiritual child, who in the first place receive your confession and grant you forgiveness, but God through me. This is his work: he receives your confession of your sins and will grant their forgiveness through our voice, as he himself declared with his own voice, speaking in his great and inexpressible love for humankind: "Whatever you bind or loose on earth will be so in heaven too: what is bound will be bound, and what is loosed will be loosed." So, as to one who knows the secrets of hearts, declare the things you have done in secret, in the presence of the holy angels, and hide nothing from me. And he who knows hidden things will blot out everything you disclose: not only what happened before and what has been done now, but also what may happen hereafter. He will enlighten your mind through the all-holy Spirit and teach you always to care for and speak the things that please him. May he give you true humility, unfeigned love, long-suffering that bears no grudge, patience and gentleness; may he put the purest fear into your heart; and, in a word, may he guide you in every kind of good work. So incline your ear, child, and listen gladly to the commands of God, who speaks to us through the holy Scriptures in this way: "Return to me, and I will heal your wounds." And again: "Do not delay in turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day, for death does not delay." And: "If a person turns from his ungodly way, he shall surely live and shall not die, and I will not remember his iniquities." And again: "Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good." And: "Confess your trespasses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed." "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." Since, then, you are admonished by the whole of Scripture and called to share in the heavenly and eternal good things, take care that, after you have renounced your lawless deeds, you never turn back to them again, and become like a dog returning to its own vomit, or a sow that has been washed going back to wallow in the mire. See, child, by the grace of Christ I have set before you what is to your benefit, and have left out nothing that serves your welfare and salvation. Now then, without delaying or being ashamed, make your declaration before God and the holy angels. For even if it seems shameful to you to uncover shameful deeds, be fully assured that through this present shame you are freed from the shame to come. And by keeping the commandments you will be counted worthy not only of forgiveness but also of crowns in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory forever. Amen. After this he has him uncover his head, as was said before, even if he should be the one who wears the crown, if it is a man; but if it is a woman, not. If it is an abba [?], he is to put his own cow- Ezek. 18:21, 22. Ps. 106:1. [?]

-l over his head, fall down before the altar, and say: "I confess to you, Father, Lord, Maker of heaven and earth, all the secrets of my heart." After he has said these words, the priest raises him up and stands him on one side of the entrance to the altar, while he himself stands on the other. Then he questions him with all cheerfulness and gentleness, and, if possible, even kisses him and places the hands of the penitent on his own neck, especially if he sees that he is distressed and overcome by unbearable grief and shame. And in a gentle and most calm voice he says to him: "Sir brother" (or "sister"), "how, first of all, was your virginity lost [?]? Through fornication, or through lawful marriage, or through masturbation, or through something against nature?" When he has acknowledged it and said that it was this way or that, he questions him again: how many women did he fall into sin with before he took a wife; were any of them slaves; how many were widows, how many married women; were any nuns, and how many; and were they of the great habit? For nuns of the small habit are judged as harlots, but those of the great habit as married women. Were any harlots, and how many; and how many were virgins? These are the first things the one who receives confessions must ask the penitent, and also how many women he fell into sin with altogether. For above all the number is sought, and the difference between the persons. There are six differences: one judgment applies to a slave woman and another to a free woman, one to a harlot and another to a virgin, one to a widow and another to a married woman, another to a nun, and another to a woman whose husband is in holy orders. He should also ask about sexual relations between males, of which there are likewise three kinds. It is one thing to have it done to one by another, which is also the lighter sin. It is another to do it to someone else, which is much heavier than having it done to one. It is another both to have it done to one by another and to do it to another, which is heavier than the two kinds already mentioned; for only having it done, or only doing it, is not as grave as both having it done and doing it. He should inquire into which of these kinds he has fallen, and how often, and over how long a period; whether before he took a wife or after he took one; whether before the age of thirty or afterwards. Also about bestiality, of which there is one kind. Likewise about masturbation, of which there are two kinds: one performed with one's own hand, the other with another's, which the lords wretchedly practice with one another, besides ruining others, those whom they have taught this abomination. Likewise about the tangled, many-wiled and deeply dark sin of incest, of which there are not one or two kinds but many and various. For it is one thing to fall into sin with two sisters, by the same father or the same mother or by both; another with a first cousin; another with a second cousin; another with a son's wife or a brother's wife; another with a mother-in-law or with the mother-in-law of one's child; and another with a stepmother or

any of his father's concubines. Some even go as far as their own mothers. It is another thing again with his own co-sponsor, and another with the girl whom he received as a goddaughter. Many also commit the abomination of male intercourse with their own wives. He should likewise inquire about murder, voluntary and involuntary; whether he has insulted his parents, or struck them, or reviled them; whether he has received communion after eating or drinking; whether he defiled himself during Lent; whether he received communion without distinction after having intercourse with a woman; whether he made a clandestine marriage, or engaged in kisses and touching without completing the act; whether he has corrupted a boy; whether he has withheld anyone's wages; whether he has ever slandered anyone, or insulted or wronged anyone unjustly; whether he has eaten blood, or what was strangled, or killed by wild beasts, or died of itself, or was struck down by birds; whether he has been found in divination, or magic, or sorcery; and whether any thought of heresy has come to him; whether he bears envy or a grudge against anyone; whether he has sworn falsely, or stolen, or seized another's property, or received someone's deposit and denied it; whether he has borne false witness, or insulted a priest or his co-sponsor. In short, he should inquire about everything with all exactness, for it is possible for someone to have engaged in every kind of evil practice. When he has examined and ascertained everything, then for each thing he hears the penitent confess and admit, he must say: "May God forgive you." And after enumerating everything and receiving the confession, while the one who has confessed lies prostrate, he adds again: "May our Master and Lord Jesus Christ, God, forgive you all that you have declared before him to my nothingness." Another absolution. "God, who through Nathan forgave David the evils he confessed, and Peter when he wept bitterly over his denial, and the harlot who wept at his spotless feet, and Manasseh, and the tax collector and the prodigal; who said, 'Confess your trespasses to one another': may he, our Savior and our Lord Jesus Christ, forgive you all that you have declared before him to my lowliness, in this present age and in the age to come; and may he count you worthy to stand uncondemned before his judgment seat, he who is blessed forever."
Another absolution. "God, who for our sake became man and bears the sins of the whole world, may he by his own

[?] receive [?] all that you have now declared before him to my unworthiness, forgiving you everything, both in this present age and in the age to come, he who wills, ensures and bestows the salvation of all, who is blessed forever. Amen." Then he prays as follows: "O God our Savior, who through your prophet

[?] Nathan granted forgiveness to David when he repented of his offenses, and who accepted Manasseh's prayer of repentance: accept your servant N. too, who has repented and confessed his trespasses, with your accustomed compassion. For you, Lord, are the one who commanded us to forgive those who fall into sin even seventy times seven; for as is your majesty, so also is your mercy. You are the God of those who repent, who relent over all our wickedness, and to you we send up glory, to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, now." "Master, Lord God, who call the righteous to sanctification and sinners to be justified: accept the repentance of your servant N., and as he falls down before your majesty confessing the sins he has committed, set him free, for you are good. Redeem him from every sin of the flesh. Make him shine clean from every soiled conscience; cleanse him and strengthen him in keeping your commandments; count him worthy of the forgiveness of his sins, so that the Holy Spirit, dwelling in him through purity of soul and body, may make him an heir of the kingdom of heaven, by the grace, compassion and love for humankind of your only-begotten Son, with whom you are blessed, together with your all-holy, good and life-giving Spirit, now." "Lord God of the salvation of your servants, merciful and compassionate, long-suffering and abounding in mercy, who relent over our wickedness, who do not desire the death of the sinner but rather that he should turn and live: be entreated now too for your servant N., and grant him pardon of sins and expiation of iniquities, forgiving him every offense, voluntary and involuntary. Be reconciled to him and unite him to your holy Church in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom to you belong power, majesty and magnificence, together with the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, now." "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, Lamb and Shepherd, who take away the sin of the world; who canceled the debt of the two debtors and gave forgiveness of sins to the sinful woman; who granted healing to the paralytic together with the forgiveness of his sins: Master, remit, pardon and forgive the iniquities, the sins, the offenses, the voluntary ones, those done knowingly and in ignorance, those committed in disobedience and transgression by your servant N. And if, as a man who bears flesh and lives in this world, he has transgressed or offended through the [?] of the devil, whether in word or in deed, whether knowingly or in ignorance, whether in the matter of heresy; whether he has come under a curse, or fallen under his own anathema or an oath: do you, as a good, loving and forgiving Master, overlook it, and be pleased that he be loosed by your word, forgiving him at once both his own anathema and the oath, according to your inexpressible love for humankind. Master, Lord our God, hear

me as I entreat your goodness, and overlook all his failings, for you abound in mercy; and deliver him from eternal punishment. For you said, Master, 'Whomever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven too, and whomever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven too.' For you are God without sin, and able to forgive sins, and to you we send up glory, together with your Father who is without beginning and your all-holy, good and life-giving Spirit, now and always and forever." "Father, Lord, do not deliver your servant N. into the hands of the devil, so that our enemies may not attack us. Set on his mouth the keeping of your commandments, and on his lips a hidden seal, so that he may not speak deceit. Thrust a proud eye far from him; cleanse wantonness and wickedness from his soul; let no harsh and proud spirit or deceitful tongue be in him. Set a good spirit over his mind, Lord, and cleanse him from every unclean spirit. Shake off from him all misery; forgive him every debt of sins. Look down from heaven and gladden him, for he has hoped in you. Strengthen him with the power of your Holy Spirit, and do not let him be swallowed up by the devil, for you have [?] us from eternal death through the grace of your Christ, with whom you are blessed, together with your all-holy, good and life-giving Spirit, now." Then he raises him up, embraces him and urges him to be of good cheer, saying to him: "See, by the will of God, who loves humankind and wills the salvation of all, you have run to repentance and made your confession, and you have been freed from all your former evil deeds. So do not, through neglect of the divine commandments, throw yourself into further evils, lest, as the Gospel says, your last state become worse than the first, from which you have been redeemed through God's love for humankind. Rather, strive as far as you are able to keep the Lord's commandments, and so attain salvation." Then the priest says: "Wisdom. The reading from the prophet Ezekiel. Thus says the Lord Almighty: If the lawless person turns away from all the iniquities he has committed, and keeps all my commandments, and does righteousness and mercy, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of the trespasses he has committed shall be remembered; in the righteousness he has done he shall live. Do I indeed desire the death of the lawless? says the Lord; is it not rather that he should turn from his evil way and live? But when the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and does injustice, according to all the iniquities the lawless person has done, none of the righteous deeds he has done shall be remembered; in the trespass he has committed and in the sins he has sinned, in them

he shall die. Yet you said, 'The way of the Lord is not right.' Hear now, all the house of Israel: is it my way that is not right? Is it not your way that is not right? When the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits a trespass and dies in the trespass he has committed, in it he shall die. And when the lawless person turns away from the lawlessness he has committed and does justice and righteousness, he has kept his soul; he has turned away from all the ungodly deeds he has done, he shall surely live and shall not die, says the Lord Almighty." "The Gospel according to Luke. At that time all the tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying, 'This man receives sinners and eats with them.' So he told them this parable: 'Which of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that is lost until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them, "Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost." I tell you that in the same way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance. Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and search carefully until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, "Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost." Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.'" Then, having said the Trisagion, and again the troparia in the fourth tone, "Visit my lowly soul" and another, "Sailing across the sea," and "Let us now run earnestly to the Mother of God," and then saying "Lord, be merciful" three times, and likewise "Lord, forgive" and "Lord, have mercy on us," and having made forty prostrations, both are dismissed. After completing the rite set out above, the priest sits down with him and says: "Child, what are you able to keep?" For penances are given according to the strength and willingness of the one who receives them, and not in proportion to the sins he has committed. It may be that one who has sinned little but is eager should receive a heavy penance, so that he may obtain not only forgiveness of sins but also a crown; while one who has sinned much but is lax should have a light penance, so that he is not swallowed up by its weight and, growing lax, give up everything. For we were commanded to lighten burdens, not to impose burdens [?]. For the yoke of Christ is easy, and his burden is light. With compassion he must also take into account the differences of persons, of times, of places, of knowledge and igno-

…[?], and in everything to follow the aim of the saints [?]. For the divine Chrysostom says: “Repentance is judged not by time, but by the disposition of the soul.” In agreement with him the great Basil also says: “We do not judge such things by time, but we attend to the manner of repentance.” Further, the most loving Chrysostom says: “The Ninevites did not need many days to repent, but only three. And the thief did not need even so many hours: the interval of the single word he spoke was enough for his repentance, so that in an instant he came to be in paradise.” Knowing this, then, one should set penances not according to the strictness of the divine canons, but according to the character of the person. And [?] this concerns men. In the case of women, one must make a great deal of inquiry and take great care. For they go as far as magic, sorcery with potions, and other shameful acts that are dreadful even to mention, let alone to commit. They also defile their husbands without the husbands knowing, through intercourse during their monthly periods. When these women confess, however, their heads must not be uncovered, for that is prescribed for men. Women also go as far as various kinds of murder, both in conception and even in full-term births. Some of them commit murder every month by means of a certain herb; I, the lowly one, have had to receive this pitiable confession too, along with all those written above. For this reason, after going through everything else, one must ask how many children they killed (nuns above all), and by what means, and how many times. For it is one thing to drink a drug so as never again to bear children, which is the heaviest of all; and another to use ground preparations, which is lighter than the one just mentioned. But to expel an embryo every month by means of an herb is the most savage [?] of all murders, and it carries the penance of not communing even until death, unless she cuts it off. When women are excluded [?], let them make only bows in church, without prostrations. And women too practise masturbation, like men, even those who remain virgins and have no experience of a man whatsoever. So much, then, for careful inquiry into those who confess, and the differences among them.

The penances and their distinctions are these. Whatever was done before the age of thirty, whether by men or by women, should be easily pardoned and quickly forgiven, whatever it may be, so that the penance extends to two or three years, provided there is no murder of any kind nor grave incest. If the sins took place after the age of thirty, the penance should extend to three or four years. But where there is a murder, or several murders, or one of the higher degrees of incest, namely with a full sister (that is, of the same father and mother), or with a son's wife, or with a co-parent, or in the case of those who take two sisters in marriage, or who are mad with lust for their stepmothers: twelve years. But if it happens with a daughter whom they received, or with one's own mother, or

PENITENTIAL. with one's own daughter: sixteen years. If someone has sinned only according to nature and has not fallen into unnatural acts, nor into incest of any kind or degree, let him be penanced for up to a year, or a year and a half. But if, in the case of a woman, various murders and sorceries were committed, or even unnatural acts, let them be penanced for up to eight or ten years. We set these distinctions and penances in regard to communion. For the heaviest sin of all is to commune unworthily. It escaped us to say that those who confess should be asked, after the whole confession of their sins, whether they were receiving communion while doing the things they have just confessed. If someone says “Yes,” and especially outside Pascha, this is worse than everything else, even if the transgression, that is, the sin, is among the least; and the abstention from the immaculate communion should be made longer. As for food, drink and prayer, these depend on what each person's nature, mind, choice, strength and disposition can bear. For the present we have two distinctions, by which we both determine and give penances to those who confess to us, whatever the sins may be and of whatever kind, both for those who have sinned greatly and for those who have sinned slightly. For we said earlier that whether penances are given lightly or heavily depends both on those who confess and on those who receive the confession. The unhesitating faith of the one confessing, and his sharing of what he has, which the blessed Apostle somewhere calls the fruit of faith [?], together with the well-balanced judgment, knowledge and compassionate condescension of the one who receives the penitent, can make everything light, whether in food, drink or communion, especially if the penitent has stopped sinning before confessing [?], or at least promises to cut it off from the time of his confession. For there are many who confess and grieve, yet whether by nature, or by being taken unawares, or by perverse will, or by evil habit, they slip again and fall into sins. Such people, then, should confess every time they fall. And if they fulfil their penances, however many years they received from the one who bound them, and having completed them are about to commune, let them commune then, if they are at all shown mercy; but let them be wary of the immaculate communion until they cut the sin off. For on this account alone will they be counted worthy of mercy at the judgment. Since, however, there are some who through the force of habit cannot restrain themselves even in Great Lent (and these are often men who have wives), it is necessary that they too, after fulfilling their penances, if many years go by and they have no way to commune because they keep falling into sins, should at least keep holy Lent

in its entirety without sinning, and then with fear and trembling let them commune on the three days of Pascha. We say this is done out of necessity, because they are never able to restrain themselves from [fleshly?] defilements, and not by reason of any other distinction. But if such people fall into masturbation in Great Lent, let them not commune even then. For in the case of this pitiable passion, which overpowers everyone and is so hard to give up, our holy Fathers prescribed only forty days without communion for those who fall into it; yet this was fixed for the other days of the year, not for the days of holy Lent. Concerning food, drink and prayer.

These two, then, as I said above, are in my judgment the two distinctions of penances, which I, the lowly one, am accustomed [?] to give to everyone: to those of many sins, the sick, the young and the old, women and men, monks and nuns, with the exception of those in holy orders. For priests and bishops and ordained deacons, or their wives, should not be received for confession unless they first assure before God those who receive them that, if they have any charge that bars them, that is, that stops them from exercising the priesthood, they will no longer dare to [?] serve. For to such people no penance of any kind is given, no restriction at all of food, drink or communion, but only cessation from the priesthood. Nothing stops a priest from celebrating except this alone: if he falls with another woman besides his lawful wife. For if he falls with one woman, and only once, he no longer has authority ever to celebrate, even if he could strive so hard as to raise the dead. There are other defilements, however, into which, if a priest falls, especially a monk or one of those ordained without a wife, he receives a temporary suspension from the priesthood, that is, from celebrating, and then celebrates again. As the blessed Basil says concerning deacons and presbyters: “A deacon defiled in the lips, who confesses that he has sinned to this extent, shall be withheld from the liturgy, but shall be counted worthy to partake of communion with the deacons. The same applies to a presbyter. But if anyone is found to have sinned beyond this, let him be deposed, whatever rank he holds.” What does “defiled in the lips” mean? I do not write it, though I know it clearly. The one who has done it will make it plain. However, concerning the priests of whom we have spoken, and also concerning those worthy to come to sacred office, and concerning laypeople, how far these matters extend and by what standards they are judged, come, let us speak briefly, as far as we are able and as far as we know. Those men or women who without necessity, that is, without fear of men or poverty, were defiled with the bodies of pagans: if they are men without lawful wives, or women [without?] lawful husbands, let them be without communion for three years, together with the things written below

concerning food, drink and prayer by way of penance, whichever and whatever kind they choose from the three. Those who have lawful wives, or women who have husbands, should be penanced for four or five years, especially if they happen to have fallen into other sins as well. But if it happened under fear and coercion, or because of poverty, let them be penanced for one year or two. The wives of clergy, that is, of deacons or presbyters, whenever they fall, should be penanced for three years, as having murdered their priests; for those men will no longer celebrate if they choose to have relations with their wives even once. Priests and deacons, whenever they fall, even if the fall happens only once, should no longer celebrate at all; but let them commune whenever they wish, and hold the rank of reader, doing without shame whatever a reader knows how to do. If a reader falls, or his wife, the reader may no longer advance further, but must remain without promotion. If someone, while still a child, whether in the secular or the monastic order, or even a priest's son [?], is corrupted by some man: if it was only between the thighs, he should be penanced, and severely, if it happened once or twice; but if more than this, that is, in the anus, he must not come at all to the dignity of ordained deacon or priest. For even if he did not sin, the vessel was nevertheless broken, and it is not permissible for him to celebrate, for he has been defiled. If someone falls into masturbation before being ordained, not knowing what it is or that it bars him from receiving the priesthood, whether out of ignorance or because he was taught it by some other soul-destroying or ignorant person, and the man is wise, or devout, or both, let him first be penanced, and then be counted worthy. But if he was caught in this after ordination, in the way we described above, either through ignorance or because he was taught by a soul-destroyer that it is not evil, let him receive a year of penance, being kept from celebrating, and then celebrate. But if he does it a second or third time, let him no longer celebrate, but pass to the order of reader. If someone has committed major thefts, let him not come to the priesthood. Likewise, if he does so after ordination, let him no longer celebrate. In the same way, those not in holy orders who steal should never come to the priesthood, but should receive the penance of fornicators. Among those who confess, there are in my experience ten types, differing from one another. One is the person who sinned a little and repented of his own free will, and with only one person. Another is the one caught many times and with many persons. Another sinned according to nature, perhaps with one person, but persisted in it until old age. Another sinned against nature but cut it off quickly through the fear of God. Another came to confession because of sickness or the pressure of misfortune, or [?] confessed at the very point of death, and died [?]. And another, having stopped

to say with how many persons he fell, that is, with how many women; and likewise the women too. Then the one who receives their confession in God should examine them as to what kinds of persons these were, among the six varieties of fornication: that is, how many were prostitutes, how many widows, how many nuns of the small habit, how many nuns of the great habit, and how many clergy wives, that is, presbyters' wives or wives of ordained deacons. For nuns of the small habit, and the wives of readers, are judged as prostitutes, while those of the great habit are judged as married women. When those confessing have stated the varieties and numbers of these, and how long they persisted in each passion, and whether any children were born of them or not, and whether they had wives or not, and whether they sinned according to nature or in both ways, and how often, and whether they cut it off, or went on sinning until old age, or cut it off earlier: when he has stated the varieties of all these, then ask them again about incest, in case they fell with any relatives or [?]. And if he finds them guilty in any of these, ask them whether they turned back from the second person of the kinship to the first again or not, for this is worse. After that, examine them about unnatural sins: whether they fell with a man, or a child, or a beast, or a bird, or a girl before the appointed age of sixteen. Then about voluntary and involuntary murder, together with the terrible double [that is, mutual] masturbation. And when he has examined the penitent well on all these points, then, according to his strength, or rather according to his compunction, his humility, his tears, the almsgiving he promises or has the means to give to God, and finally according to his fervent faith and resolve, give him in writing his command, that is, his penance. As for communion, as was said above, set the term at one year, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven; as for food and drink, according to each person's nature and strength. As for the liturgy, he should go out of the church with the catechumens and stand in the

PENITENTIAL. narthex. At vespers, matins and the other services, however, he may without any hindrance stand wherever he likes in the church and do whatever he likes. At the Nativity of Christ, at Epiphany, and on the three days of Pascha, that is, Holy Thursday, Holy Saturday and Holy Sunday, and on the commemoration of the Holy Apostles, he may partake, in place of communion [?], of the holy water of Epiphany, and so break the fast: the monks with cheese and eggs, the others with meat as well. For the present I hold to three distinctions in what concerns food and drink when I penance anyone. For the same strictness, discernment and judgment ought to apply to women and to men, to those in the world and to monastics, with the exception of male and female slaves. For male and female slaves have been regulated by the divine canons to receive only half the penance, because they are not under their own authority. This, then, is the first rule of penance for all, except male and female slaves, that I give to everyone: on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, to eat oil and pulses with vegetables only, and to abstain from cheese, eggs, meat and fish; on Tuesday and Thursday, to eat everything freely except meat. On Saturday and Sunday they are not to be penanced in any food or drink whatever, but are to be free in everything, like all who have no penance, that is, free to eat meat, drink wine, and everything else. Likewise on every feast of the Lord and of the all-holy Theotokos, and of the twelve Apostles, whichever of them it may be and whatever day it falls on, the penitent is free in food and drink; and on such a feast he need not keep Wednesday or Friday. The same applies to the feast of the Forerunner, the Twelve Days, Easter week, and the week after Pentecost, which we call the week of the Holy Spirit. As for the days from Antipascha to Pentecost, in them they are entirely released in everything except Wednesday and Friday, on which they keep a single restriction: those in the world abstain from meat, the monks from cheese and eggs. The two weeks of Meatfare and of the Prophonesimos are also to be free in everything for all, the monks for cheese and eggs, those in the world for meat, except on their Wednesdays and Fridays. These days they should then keep entirely pure, if possible even without fish, and fast until evening. For this too is always laid down by the divine canon, as has been said, except on a feast, during the Twelve Days and in the Pentecost season: they are not to break the fast in any way even for the sake of a friend, unless perhaps because of illness or some other serious circumstance. Those under penance should, if possible, always keep a measure for wine, except on Saturday, Sunday and feasts; and for the present, without exception, on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, that is, to drink one litra a day. If anyone is able to drink no wine at all on these three days, he has a great reward. Nevertheless,

the nature, mind or character of each will be discerned by the one who receives him, and he will determine whether he may drink more than the measure. For the two Lents, that of Saint Philip and that of the Holy Apostles, we decree that those in the world should not partake of meat, nor monks of cheese and eggs, except, if they wish, at the solstice feast of the Forerunner and at the Entry into the Holy of Holies, and these only if any ask for them. In Great Lent, if possible, those in the world should not partake of fish, except on Saturday and Sunday, and the monks not of oil. If they do not choose this, then for now they may break the fast only on Tuesday and Thursday, the former with fish, the latter with oil. Unless they are bedridden, if possible they should not even drink wine except on Saturday and Sunday. But if they are pressed by faintheartedness, or love of pleasure, or many reasonable causes, and do not choose this, then for now on Monday, Wednesday and Friday all who choose to repent should not touch wine, and above all should not drink it at all during the whole first week. In the last week, that is, Holy Week, they may drink a little, and only on Holy Thursday. This, with me, is the first rule, which also covers the distinctions for the other seasons of the whole year. The second is this: if the penitents cannot keep this rule, or rather do not choose to, let them keep Wednesdays and Fridays completely pure. That is, those in the world should not taste meat, cheese, eggs or fish, but only oil, pulses and vegetables; and the monks, unless they are sick, not even oil. On the other five days of the week all are to be free in everything, so that each may eat according to his calling: that is, those in the world everything, including cheese, eggs and milk. The third rule, adopted out of necessity, is this: if they will not follow even this, whether through love of pleasure, vainglory or sickness, let them keep these two days of the week completely pure during the time of their penance, as has been said, but the monks may eat oil and those in the world fish. I know that for these very compassionate dispensations I shall be condemned before the common Judge and God of all; but even so, it is better for me to be condemned for such things than to be praised as one without compassion. As for prayers, they should pray three times in the course of a day and night: in the morning, when they are about to eat, at the hour of supper, and when they go to sleep. At each prayer those who know it should say the [?], the Trisagion, the Our Father, “Lord, have mercy” a hundred times, “O God, be merciful to me a sinner” eight times, and make eight prostrations. Those who do not choose to do this, or cannot, should do at least half of it; and those who cannot do even that, a third. On all Saturdays and Sundays, on feasts and during the Twelve Days, and likewise on the days from Pascha to All Saints, they should not kneel at prayer, but only make bows in every case.

PENITENTIAL [?]. These, then, are the rules for the very small and most lenient penances that I have imposed and still impose. Basil the Great gave us support for this comparison when he said: “We write all these things so that the fruits of repentance may be tested. For we do not judge such matters simply by length of time, but we pay attention to the manner of the repentance.” Anyone entrusted by the loving-kindness of God with the power to loose and to bind will not deserve condemnation if he shows greater mercy and shortens the period of penance, seeing that the sinner’s confession goes beyond what is required. For the history in the Scriptures shows us that those who confess with greater anguish quickly obtain God’s loving-kindness. “But if they can hardly be torn away from their own habits, and choose to serve their pleasures rather than the Lord, and will not accept the life according to the Gospel, we have nothing in common with them. For among a disobedient and contrary people we have been taught to hear: ‘Save your own soul and be saved.’” Let us not consent, then, to perish together with others in their sins. Rather, let us fear the heavy judgment, keep the dreadful day before our eyes, and refuse to perish together with such people. For to our good God be glory to the ages of ages. Amen. A prayer for one who has been bound [?] by a priest and [?]

Compassionate, good and loving Lord, in your mercies you sent your only-begotten Son into the world to tear up [?] the record of debt that stood against us, to loose the bonds of those shackled by sin, and to proclaim release to captives, having destroyed the sting of death. Now, Master, in your goodness free this your servant here present from the yoke laid upon him. Loosen the bond that has been placed on him, and grant him to approach your majesty without sin, at every time and in every place, with boldness and a pure conscience, and to ask for your abundant mercy. For you are a merciful God who loves humankind, and to you we offer up glory, to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages.
